messages.subject_clean: [GGIR] Re: output part 4- how to get summary based on filenames similar to output part2
messages.body_plain:
Hi both,

In the latest GGIR release on GitHub 2.7-5 this has been addressed. GGIR part 4 output is now split based on recording name and not based on participant ID. For cross-sectional studies this should make not difference, but for longitudinal studies you should be able to study each recording separately in the results.

Best, Vincent

For exporting time series with detected sleep included see documentation for GGIR arguments "save_ms5rawlevels", "save_ms5raw_without_invalid" and "save_ms5raw_format".

This happens in GGIR part 5 because that is where GGIR constructs time series of the detection, in contrast to GGIR part 4 where the focus is only on start- and end- times.

Cheers, Vincent

messages.body_plain:
> However, we will fix this in some way.
​

If you observe unexpected behaviour then it is important that you try to help fix it. For example, by sharing a detailed description of the issue and in case you find a solution by proposing that solution to us.

Open-source projects like GGIR depend on an ongoing effort from the community to report and address problems. Once everyone starts to make their own local ad-hoc fixes to problems it will hugely limit the growth and quality of GGIR.

Just like you are benefitting from the endless hours others have put into GGIR, others will be grateful if you could also share your experiences. Detailed bug reports help.

Thanks,

Vincent

Dr. Vincent van Hees | Independent consultant | https://accelting.com/

Hi Gengze,

Sleep efficiency isn't calculated within GGIR unless you have used a sleep log or when using guider HorAngle for hip-worn accelerometer data. If either of these applies set argument sleepwindowType to “TimeInBed”. See this info in section 4.2.1.1 in the vignette: https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/GGIR/vignettes/GGIR.html

Alternatively, you can just calculate this yourself in the nightsummary.csv as:
Sleepefficiency = SleepDurationInSpt /  SptDuration

Kind regards,
Ben

Hello,

I’m using GGIR (v 2.7-1) to analyse AX6 Axivity data.  We have 600+ *.cwa data files, which have 7 days

The GGIR function runs successfully with no errors, but I have
very large clipping scores in the part2summary – the average is 0.65, with 99% of values greater
than 0.01. According to the vignette the clipping score 'should be 0'.

The data are from 100 accelerometers, so it’s unlikely that
they’re all faulty, and the dynamic range is set to the default 8g. Looking at
a few of the datasets in OmGUI doesn’t show any obvious issues with the data.

I'm running this on a Linux high performance cluster, but get the same problem on Windows 10 with default parameters: GGIR(datadir=acceldir, outputdir=outputdir)

 I have a suspicion it's to do with the gyroscope data - has anyone else had problems with AX6 data when collecting gyroscope data, or found a solution?

Thanks,

Ruth

Actually, being able to read a .gt3x file with read.gt3x::read.gt3x() does not guarantee that GGIR can read it.

The read.gt3x package can read both older and newer .gt3x files. However, only for the newer format we implemented the option to read the data in batches <https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/read.gt3x/vignettes/batch_loading_gt3x.html>. GGIR needs that batch reading functionality, by which GGIR can only process newer .gt3x files.

By new I mean firmware of 2.5.0 or higher and serial numbers starting with CLE, MOS or TAS: https://github.com/actigraph/GT3X-File-Format. If I understood correctly these are the devices that have been sold since 2017-isch.

A better test would be read.gt3x::read.gt3x(file = "file.gt3x", batch_begin = 1, batch_end =2), because that will trigger an error if it is an old file that GGIR cannot handle but read.gt3x possibly can.
Best,
Vincent

Hi Alicia,

I will chime in here because I had a similar question awhile back using the same AX3 device. I reached out directly to the people at Newcastle who developed the AX3, and unfortunately they alerted me to the fact that the light sensor on the AX3 is not meant for functional use. This was a major disappointment to me too! Here is a copy of the response I received from Dan Jackson, one of the engineers on the project:

"The light sensor is perhaps only really suitable as a general, relative, indicator of light, for example to distinguish a varying/stable, or rising/falling level, or general pattern over a day.  The sensor is not used with a light pipe to the surface, so light is filtered in through the case and potting material, so may have inter-device variability and a complicated response with angle where the light may be diffused, and is easily obscured by the wearer’s clothing etc.  In addition, as a secondary sensor, the value has a rather complicated update cycle (updated once a second, but only stored once for every 80/120 unpacked/packed accelerometer samples).

Overall, I’m afraid it’s not suitable for quantitative measurements on its own."

Hope this helps,

Tom

Hi Adithy,

GGIR does not provide nap estimates, but reports time spent in sustained inactivity bouts (abbreviated as sib). I intentionally named it like that because there is no evidence that these reflect naps. For example, they could also reflect brief episodes of sensor non-wear.

Unfortunately, authors like https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34637446/ and https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-020-20585-3 ignored that and referred to sibs as 'naps', because that makes it easier to score publications or something, but it is not evidence based

We do have some prototype code for nap detection in 3-4 year olds based on waist worn accelerometer data, which I would not recommend you to use and which I therefore have not documented well yet.
Best, Vincent

messages.subject_clean: [GGIR] Re: Part 4 sleep efficiency
messages.body_plain:
Thanks Ben for jumping in.

Just wanted to clarify that:

> sleep_efficiency = SleepDurationInSpt/SptDuration
​
is not entirely in line with how the sleep research community defines sleep efficiency. The official definition is to also include sleep latency. However, because we do not have sleep latency in many GGIR applications (without sleep log that asks the person when they went to bed) you could argue that the above calculation is at least some attempt to quantify sleep efficiency. However, be aware that the values will differ between both definitions and report that this is how it is calculated.

In earlier version of GGIR I used this definition of sleep efficiency in GGIR part4 output. When I became aware of the inconsistency with what sleep researchers do, I removed it from part4 output which now only shows sleep efficiency if sleep latency is known.

I believe the latency-free sleep efficiency is still part of part 5 output,  so in that sense I have not been entirely consistent.

In other words, part 4 output is an attempt to align with terminology and definitions of sleep research, while part 5 output is more aimed at a general audience interested in 24 hour time use.

Best, Vincent

On Monday, 19 September 2022 at 23:29:53 UTC+5:30 Vincent van Hees wrote:
> Thanks Ben for jumping in.
>
> Just wanted to clarify that:
>
> > sleep_efficiency = SleepDurationInSpt/SptDuration
> ​
> is not entirely in line with how the sleep research community defines sleep efficiency. The official definition is to also include sleep latency. However, because we do not have sleep latency in many GGIR applications (without sleep log that asks the person when they went to bed) you could argue that the above calculation is at least some attempt to quantify sleep efficiency. However, be aware that the values will differ between both definitions and report that this is how it is calculated.
>
> In earlier version of GGIR I used this definition of sleep efficiency in GGIR part4 output. When I became aware of the inconsistency with what sleep researchers do, I removed it from part4 output which now only shows sleep efficiency if sleep latency is known.
>
> I believe the latency-free sleep efficiency is still part of part 5 output,  so in that sense I have not been entirely consistent.
>
> In other words, part 4 output is an attempt to align with terminology and definitions of sleep research, while part 5 output is more aimed at a general audience interested in 24 hour time use.
>
> Best, Vincent

messages.body_plain:
Hi Glenn, ENMO is typically averaged over 5 second bins, so it's common to read this in the literature. GGIR does make it customisable by changing the arguments in windowsizes. for example I have used 1s and 60s epochs for various reasons such as investigating short duration movements or aligning it with other data which was saved at a different epoch.

Kind regards,
Ben

Would we take say the L5hr from 01/02/2022 and pair this with the questionnaire from 02/02/2022 or is the ENMO readout on from calendar_date 02/02/2022 corresponding to the previous nights L5 onset?
